analysis.one_liner: Requires automatic federal approval of all natural gas imports and exports, ending public-interest review.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have stripped regulators of their power to deny or condition natural gas exports, died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the Department of Energy must find that exporting natural gas to countries without a free-trade agreement is in the public's interest before approving it. This bill would have rewritten that rule so that every export and import license is granted "without modification or delay," and would have barred any federal official from restricting or conditioning natural gas trade. The President would keep narrow powers to limit exports during a declared disaster or a national emergency involving a specific country. The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas producers and LNG export companies gain the most: their export applications would be approved automatically, with no public-interest test, no delay, and virtually no conditions, opening the door to shipping more domestic gas to foreign buyers at international prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gas producers and LNG export companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Natural Gas Act so that export and import authorizations must be issued "without modification or delay," removing the Energy Department's power to deny, condition, or slow them.

It strikes the existing export-approval framework (subsections (b) and (c) of the Natural Gas Act) and adds a blanket prohibition: no federal employee may impose or enforce any restriction or condition on natural gas exports or imports, outside the narrow emergency exceptions.

It directs the Energy Secretary to report within 180 days on actions to "foster" natural gas exports and to identify regulations that "inhibit" the export market, framing federal policy around expanding exports.
The bill's own findings declare that exporting U.S. natural gas is in the national interest and may lower global carbon emissions by displacing higher-emitting fuels abroad.

analysis.who_pays: American buyers of natural gas — households that heat with it, electric utilities, and gas-dependent manufacturers — would bear the cost. Once exports are unrestricted, domestic prices link to higher international prices, since exporters will pay up to world rates. The Energy Department and Congress also lose oversight of who ships gas where.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and manufacturers buying natural gas

drawbacks.text: Removing the public-interest test means unlimited export applications must be approved on demand, which pulls domestic natural gas toward higher world prices — raising heating bills, electricity costs, and feedstock costs for gas-reliant manufacturers.

The bill strips regulators of discretion to weigh domestic supply, price effects, or national-security concerns case by case, leaving only a 90-day presidential limit after a declared disaster or a country-specific emergency.

Supporters' counterargument, written into the bill's findings, is that exports expand gas production, support jobs in producing states, and cut global emissions by displacing coal and other fuels overseas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a clean win for gas producers and exporters and a clear cost shift onto American gas consumers, who would pay world-market prices for a fuel they now buy largely at domestic prices. The environmental and jobs arguments are speculative and unquantified in the bill, while the price effect on U.S. households and industry is direct. The narrow emergency carve-outs do not restore meaningful public-interest oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on June 22, 2017.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which was its only action in the Senate.
The committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: American natural gas consumers — households, electric utilities, and gas-dependent manufacturers — are better off because the bill died, since the Department of Energy keeps its authority to review exports for the public interest before approving them. LNG exporters simply continue operating under the existing approval process, which the bill's text says would remain untouched for permits already in effect.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require automatic approval of natural gas exports and imports.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing or markup, so it never advanced to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors and no recorded floor or committee votes, so no partisan split can be measured; it simply never moved.

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and LNG export companies
industries.note: The bill would have made export approvals automatic and untouchable, letting exporters ship gas to foreign buyers paying world prices. Because that bidding raises the price U.S. consumers pay for the same gas, the industry's gain here comes directly out of ordinary households' and manufacturers' pockets.
Unrestricted exports would raise their fuel and feedstock costs as domestic prices converge with higher international prices, costs that flow through to consumers' bills and goods prices.
The bill strips the Energy Department of its authority to deny, condition, or review gas trade, leaving it with only reporting duties on how to foster exports.
